title: Ambush and instinctive shooting
summary: How ambush works and why the trigger is pulled before the target reaches the point, when it can help, and what instinctive shooting means.

body.html: Ambush, or spot shooting, is the opposite of a swing. 1) The muzzles are placed at a point ahead of the target, on its line, close to the break point. 2) They wait with little or no movement. 3) The trigger is pulled before the target reaches that spot. The shooter’s reaction and the flight of the shot both take time, so the target flies into the shot. Firing only when the target arrives at the spot sends the shot behind it.
The muzzles wait still ahead of the rabbit; the shot must come before it reaches them, or it goes behind.
body.heading: Watch how the lead works

body.html: In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ the gun may be mounted only once the target has appeared. So an ambush there always starts with a mount: the stock comes up as the muzzles go to the waiting point, and the swing is very small.

As a general habit, typical of untrained shooters, it is unreliable: the gun is still and the timing must be very precise. But a deliberate ambush is sometimes the right choice: a target that must be taken very fast, or a rabbit visible only in a short gap between bushes. A close relative is the “collapse”, used on a battue (a thin, flat clay that flies fast on its edge, then turns and drops) at the top of its flight. The barrels wait almost where the battue will be broken, so the gun has to move only a little when the shot comes. In Sporting™ the target must still be broken where the referee can see it.

In instinctive shooting the shooter does not think about lead at all. The eyes stay locked on the target (a hard focus), and the hands follow the eyes without measuring anything. Mount and swing merge into one movement, and the trigger is pulled the moment the stock settles against the cheek. The approach comes from a classic British school of game shooting.
Many top Sporting™ shooters mix methods, choosing per target. “Which method for this one?” is a normal coaching question.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: You're ambushing it — keep the gun moving with the target.
phrases.meaning: The shooter is waiting at a point; the coach wants a moving method here.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Ambush this one in the gap.
phrases.meaning: Deliberately wait at the opening and fire just before the target reaches your point, so it flies into the shot.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Don't think about the lead, just look at the bird and let the gun go to it.
phrases.meaning: Shoot instinctively: focus on the target and let the hands follow.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Hold right on the break point and just collapse onto it.
phrases.meaning: Put the muzzles almost at the break point and make only a tiny move as the battue arrives.

key_points.html: Ambush: muzzles still at a point ahead; fire before the target gets there, so it flies into the shot.
Unreliable as a habit, useful deliberately (very fast targets, short gaps).
“Collapse”: on a battue at the top of its flight, hold almost at the break point and make only a small move.
Instinctive: no thinking about lead, hard focus, mount and swing as one movement.
Good shooters choose the method per target.

options.text: The gun swings faster than the target
The gun waits at a point ahead of the target
The gun tracks the target, then accelerates
The gun starts behind the target, on its line

quiz.explain: Ambush means little or no swing: the muzzles wait on the line and the target flies into the shot.

quiz.q: When can a deliberate ambush be a good choice?

options.text: In no case: the rules forbid it
Only in Compak® Sporting, not in Sporting™
On a rabbit seen only in a short gap

quiz.explain: When the target is visible only briefly, there is no time for a swing, so waiting at the gap can work. No rule forbids any method.

options.text: Hard focus on the target, no conscious lead
Shooting from the hip, without mounting
Waiting at the trap for each target

quiz.explain: Instinctive shooting relies on eye–hand coordination; it is still done with the gun at the shoulder, as the rules require.
